claim: rrd1, rrd2, and rid4 are temperature-dependent fasciation (TDF) mutants of Arabidopsis.
source: root redifferentiation defective 1 (rrd1), rrd2, and root initiation defective 4 (rid4) are temperature-sensitive mutants of Arabidopsis that were originally isolated by us via screening using adventitious root (AR) formation from hypocotyl tissue segments as an index phenotype (Konishi and Sugiyama, 2003; Sugiyama, 2003).
evidence: The text directly states that rrd1, rrd2, and rid4 are temperature-sensitive mutants, and later refers to them as TDF mutants. This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TDF mutants form abnormally broadened (fasciated) lateral roots at 28°C but not at 22°C.
source: Most notable among these aspects was their LR phenotype, in which abnormally broadened (i.e. fasciated) LRs were formed at 28°C (non-permissive temperature), but not at 22°C (permissive temperature), in a tissue culture setting; thus, we termed the three mutants as temperature-dependent fasciation (TDF) mutants (Otsuka and Sugiyama, 2012).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the temperature-dependent LR fasciation phenotype and cites previous work.

claim: Fasciated lateral roots in TDF mutants exhibit exclusive enlargement of inner tissues.
source: It was later revealed that the early stages of LR development are likely affected in the TDF mutants, and that the fasciated LRs exhibit exclusive enlargement of inner tissues (Otsuka and Sugiyama, 2012)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and cites previous work.

claim: TDF genes encode negative regulators of cell division important for size restriction of the central zone during early stage LR primordium formation.
source: suggesting that the genes responsible for the TDF mutations (TDF genes) encode negative regulators of cell division that are important for the size restriction of the central zone during the formation of early stage LR primordia
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes described in the text.

claim: Mitochondrial RNA processing is required for limiting cell division during early lateral root organogenesis.
source: Here we show, through analysis of temperature-dependent fasciation (TDF) mutants of Arabidopsis, root redifferentiation defective 1 (rrd1), rrd2, and root initiation defective 4 (rid4), that mitochondrial RNA processing is required for limiting cell division during early lateral root (LR) organogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All TDF proteins localize to mitochondria.
source: All TDF proteins localized to mitochondria, where they were found to participate in RNA processing: RRD1 in mRNA deadenylation, and RRD2 and RID4 in mRNA editing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: RRD1 participates in mRNA deadenylation in mitochondria.
source: All TDF proteins localized to mitochondria, where they were found to participate in RNA processing: RRD1 in mRNA deadenylation, and RRD2 and RID4 in mRNA editing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: RRD2 and RID4 participate in mRNA editing in mitochondria.
source: All TDF proteins localized to mitochondria, where they were found to participate in RNA processing: RRD1 in mRNA deadenylation, and RRD2 and RID4 in mRNA editing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: LR fasciation in TDF mutants is triggered by reactive oxygen species generation caused by defective mitochondrial respiration.
source: Further analysis suggested that LR fasciation in the TDF mutants is triggered by reactive oxygen species generation caused by defective mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Local accumulation of auxin is critical for lateral root initiation.
source: The local accumulation of the phytohormone auxin is critical for LR initiation, driving LR founder cell identity acquisition and division via the degradation of the SOLITARY ROOT (SLR/IAA14) repressor, thus activating the expression of downstream genes mediated by the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTORS ARF7 and ARF19 (Lavenus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TDF mutants show an increase in the number of cells in the outermost layer of the MOL area of stage II primordia at 28°C compared to 22°C.
source: The comparison of the number of cells within the area consisting of more than one layer (MOL) (Hirota et al., 2007) between stages II and III, revealed that all TDF mutants showed an increase in this parameter in a temperature-dependent manner (Figure 1, C–E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TDF mutants show increased width of MOL and MTL areas in stage IV and V primordia at 28°C.
source: The same trend was observed in primordia at stage IV and V, for which the widths of the MOL and more than three layer (MTL) (Hirota et al., 2007) areas were quantified (Figure 1, F–H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There is no significant increase in lateral root density in TDF mutants at 28°C.
source: As there was no significant increase in LR density (Figure 1I; Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.3), LR fasciation in the TDF mutants seems to be the result of the expansion of individual primordia, as opposed to the fusion of multiple primordia because of overcrowding that is observed in some other mutants (Benitez-Alfonso et al., 2013; De Smet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with statistical analysis and supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: LR fasciation in TDF mutants is caused by expansion of individual primordia rather than fusion of multiple primordia.
source: As there was no significant increase in LR density (Figure 1I; Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.3), LR fasciation in the TDF mutants seems to be the result of the expansion of individual primordia, as opposed to the fusion of multiple primordia because of overcrowding that is observed in some other mutants (Benitez-Alfonso et al., 2013; De Smet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LR density data and comparison with other mutants.

claim: RRD1 is encoded by At3g25430.
source: This resulted in the identification of RRD1 as At3g25430, which encodes a poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN)-like protein
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and confirmed by complementation test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RRD1 encodes a poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN)-like protein.
source: This resulted in the identification of RRD1 as At3g25430, which encodes a poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN)-like protein
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on sequence analysis.

claim: RRD2 is encoded by At1g32415.
source: and RRD2 and RID4 as At1g32415 and At2g33680, respectively, both of which encode a pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein belonging to the PLS subfamily (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and confirmed by allelism test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: RID4 is encoded by At2g33680.
source: and RRD2 and RID4 as At1g32415 and At2g33680, respectively, both of which encode a pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein belonging to the PLS subfamily (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and confirmed by complementation test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: RRD2 and RID4 encode pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins belonging to the PLS subfamily.
source: and RRD2 and RID4 as At1g32415 and At2g33680, respectively, both of which encode a pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein belonging to the PLS subfamily (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At1g32415 has previously been reported as the gene responsible for the cell wall maintainer 2 (cwm2) mutation.
source: At1g32415 has previously been reported as the gene responsible for the cell wall maintainer 2 (cwm2) mutation (Hu et al., 2016); thus, we will refer to it as RRD2/CWM2 henceforth.
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature.

claim: The rrd1 mutation results in an 89-amino-acid C-terminal truncation of the 618-amino-acid RRD1 protein.
source: The rrd1 mutation results in an 89-amino-acid C-terminal truncation of the 618-amino-acid RRD1 protein; the mutant protein may be partially or conditionally functional.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on sequence analysis.

claim: The rrd1 mutant protein may be partially or conditionally functional.
source: The rrd1 mutation results in an 89-amino-acid C-terminal truncation of the 618-amino-acid RRD1 protein; the mutant protein may be partially or conditionally functional.
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of the mutation.

claim: The rrd2 and rid4 mutations create a stop codon close to the start codon and are likely to eliminate gene function.
source: As the rrd2 and rid4 mutations create a stop codon close to the start codon (Figure 2A), they are likely to eliminate gene function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the position of the mutations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: rid4-2 is a missense mutation that gives rise to a single amino acid substitution (G137R).
source: The rid4-2 mutation is a missense mutation that gives rise to a single amino acid substitution (G137R) (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), presumably causing a partial reduction of gene function.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The rid4-2 mutation presumably causes a partial reduction of gene function.
source: The rid4-2 mutation is a missense mutation that gives rise to a single amino acid substitution (G137R) (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), presumably causing a partial reduction of gene function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of the mutation.

claim: RRD1 and RID4 are strongly expressed in apical meristems and lateral root primordia in the root system.
source: For both RRD1 and RID4, strong GFP expression was mostly confined to apical meristems and LR primordia in the root system and slightly and much weaker expressions were detected in the stele and cortex/epidermis tissues, respectively (Figure 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The majority of RRD1 and RID4 proteins are localized to mitochondria.
source: At the subcellular level, in callus-derived protoplasts, fluorescence from the GFP-fusion proteins appeared punctate or granulated and was largely overlapped with signals from the mitochondrion-specific dye MitoTracker Orange, demonstrating that the majority of RRD1 and RID4 proteins are localized to mitochondria (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A small fraction of RRD1 resides in the plastid.
source: We also examined the overlap of GFP signal with chlorophyll autofluorescence in protoplasts prepared from greening-induced callus and found that a small fraction of RRD1 resides in the plastid as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Mitochondrial localization was confirmed for RRD2 by studying transient expression under the 35S promoter.
source: Although the tissue-level investigation of RRD2/CWM2 expression was unsuccessful because of the undetectable levels of the signals of RRD2::RRD2:GFP, mitochondrial localization was also confirmed for RRD2 by studying transient expression under the 35S promoter (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PARN belongs to the DEDD superfamily of deadenylases.
source: PARN belongs to the DEDD superfamily of deadenylases (Pavlopoulou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: In plants, PARN plays a role in the removal of poly(A) tails of mitochondrial mRNA.
source: In plants, however, PARN plays a distinct role in the removal of the poly(A) tails of mitochondrial mRNA (Hirayama et al., 2013; Hirayama, 2014; Kanazawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Microarray analysis of poly(A)+ RNAs from rrd1 explants showed a substantial increase in mitochondria-encoded poly(A)+ transcripts.
source: To test this possibility, we first performed a microarray analysis of poly(A)+ RNAs prepared from wild-type and rrd1 explants that had been induced to form LRs at 28°C, and found a substantial increase in mitochondria-encoded poly(A)+ transcripts in rrd1 explants (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, A to C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in mitochondrial transcript level in rrd1 is due to defective poly(A) tail removal rather than increased transcription.
source: As the majority of plant mitochondrial transcripts normally lack poly(A) tails, presumably because of swift removal after its addition (Holec et al., 2008), we suspected that the apparent sharp increase in mitochondrial transcript level might be ascribed to defective poly(A) tail removal, rather than increased transcription. In fact, a comparative analysis of polyadenylated and total RNA levels via quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) revealed a selective increase in polyadenylated transcripts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B and cited knowledge.

claim: CR-RT PCR analysis of cox1 mRNA revealed a marked increase in the polyadenylated to non-polyadenylated ratio in rrd1 compared with wild-type.
source: Furthermore, a circularized RNA (CR)-RT PCR analysis (Forner et al., 2007) of the cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (cox1) mRNA was performed to study its 3´ extremity, and revealed a marked increase in the polyadenylated to non-polyadenylated ratio in rrd1 compared with the wild-type plant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RACE-PAT assay showed that polyadenylated transcript levels were increased at higher temperature in rrd1.
source: In addition, a poly(A) test assay by rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE-PAT) (Sallés et al., 1999) showed that polyadenylated transcript levels were increased at higher temperature in rrd1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RRD1 is involved in poly(A) tail removal in mitochondrial mRNAs.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that RRD1 is involved in poly(A) tail removal in mitochondrial mRNAs, and that, in rrd1, polyadenylated mitochondrial transcripts accumulate in a temperature-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in Figure 3.

claim: In rrd1, polyadenylated mitochondrial transcripts accumulate in a temperature-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that RRD1 is involved in poly(A) tail removal in mitochondrial mRNAs, and that, in rrd1, polyadenylated mitochondrial transcripts accumulate in a temperature-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in Figure 3.

claim: The recombinant RRD1 protein did not show deadenylase activity under conditions effective for human PARN.
source: In our assay, as expected, the recombinant RRD1 protein did not show any activity in the conditions effective for human PARN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, D and E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, D and E.

claim: The RRD1 protein alone does not have deadenylase activity.
source: We concluded that the RRD1 protein alone does not have deadenylase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PARN activity assay results.

claim: RRD1 lacks three out of the four amino acids that are essential for PARN deadenylase function.
source: In previous studies, this possibility was excluded because, in contrast to canonical PARNs (including AtPARN/AHG2), RRD1 lacks three out of the four amino acids that are essential for its function as a deadenylase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Reverdatto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, citing previous literature.

claim: ags1 is a mutation of a mitochondrion-localized poly(A) polymerase (PAP), AGS1.
source: ags1 is a mutation of a mitochondrion-localized poly(A) polymerase (PAP), AGS1, which was originally identified based on its ability to counteract compromised function of AtPARN/AHG2 (Hirayama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: A substantial decrease in mitochondrial poly(A)+ transcript levels was observed in the rrd1 ags1 double mutant compared with the rrd1 AGS1 control.
source: A substantial decrease in mitochondrial poly(A)+ transcript levels was observed in the rrd1 ags1 double mutant compared with the rrd1 AGS1 control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rrd1 phenotypes, such as temperature-dependent LR fasciation and shoot and root growth retardation, were significantly alleviated in the rrd1 ags1 double mutant.
source: Moreover, rrd1 phenotypes, such as temperature-dependent LR fasciation and shoot and root growth retardation of seedlings (Sugiyama, 2003), were significantly alleviated (Figure 4, B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The accumulation of poly(A)+ mitochondrial transcripts is the primary cause of the rrd1 phenotype.
source: These results indicate that the accumulation of poly(A)+ mitochondrial transcripts is the primary cause of the rrd1 phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic suppression experiment with ags1.

claim: PPR proteins are known for their role in regulating various aspects of organellar post-transcriptional gene expression.
source: PPR proteins are known for their role in regulating various aspects of organellar post-transcriptional gene expression, such as RNA stabilization, RNA cleavage, RNA splicing, RNA editing, and translation (Barkan and Small, 2014; Hammani and Giegé, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Most PLS-class PPR proteins have been reported as C-to-U RNA editing factors.
source: RRD2 and RID4 belong to the PLS-class of PPR proteins, most of which have been reported as being C-to-U RNA editing factors (Kobayashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: C-to-U editing at ccb2-71C and ccb3-575C is almost completely abolished in rrd2.
source: A comprehensive sequence analysis of previously reported RNA editing sites using cDNA prepared from explants induced to form LRs at 28°C revealed an almost complete abolishment of C-to-U editing at two sites (cytochrome c biogenesis protein 2 (ccb2)−71C and ccb3-575C) in rrd2
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: C-to-U editing at atp4-395C, rpl5-58C, rpl5-59C, rps3-1344C, rps4-77C, and rps4-332C is almost completely abolished in rid4.
source: and at six sites (ATP synthase subunit 4 (atp4)−395C, ribosomal protein l5 (rpl5)−58C, rpl5-59C, rps3-1344C, rps4-77C, and rps4-332C) in rid4 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: The identification of ccb3-575C as an RRD2/CWM2 editing site is in agreement with a previous study of cwm2.
source: The identification of ccb3-575C as an RRD2/CWM2 editing site was in agreement with a previous study of cwm2 (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: RID4 editing sites showed incomplete editing in rid4-2, implying a partial loss of function in this mutant.
source: Editing was also completely abolished in these sites at 22°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A). RID4 editing sites showed incomplete editing in rid4-2, implying a partial loss of function in this mutant (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: Significant identity was found among the 5' upstream sequences of the editing sites that were affected in each mutant.
source: Significant identity was found among the 5' upstream sequences of the editing sites that were affected in each mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B), further suggesting that RRD2 and RID4 participate in the editing of these sites via direct contact.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claim: RRD2 and RID4 participate in the editing of their target sites via direct contact.
source: Significant identity was found among the 5' upstream sequences of the editing sites that were affected in each mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B), further suggesting that RRD2 and RID4 participate in the editing of these sites via direct contact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence similarity of upstream regions.

claim: BN-PAGE analysis revealed a substantial loss of complex V (ATP synthase complex) in rid4 at both 22°C and 28°C.
source: This revealed a substantial loss of complex V (ATP synthase complex) in rid4 at both 22°C and 28°C culture conditions (Figure 5B), likely caused by defective mRNA editing of atp4 (Figure 5A), which is a component of this protein complex.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The loss of complex V in rid4 is likely caused by defective mRNA editing of atp4.
source: This revealed a substantial loss of complex V (ATP synthase complex) in rid4 at both 22°C and 28°C culture conditions (Figure 5B), likely caused by defective mRNA editing of atp4 (Figure 5A), which is a component of this protein complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the editing defect and the role of atp4 in complex V.

claim: No noticeable differences in mitochondrial protein complexes were found in rrd1 and rrd2 by BN-PAGE.
source: No noticeable differences were found in rrd1 and rrd2.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text referring to the BN-PAGE analysis.

claim: ccb2 and ccb3 are related to cytochrome c maturation.
source: Because ccb2 and ccb3, the two mitochondrial genes that are targeted by RRD2/CWM2, are related to cytochrome c (cyt c) maturation (Giegé et al., 2008), we quantified cyt c levels in rrd2.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Cyt c levels on a per mitochondrial protein basis were decreased in rrd2 callus cultured at 28°C for 3 days in two out of three cultures.
source: Cyt c levels on a per mitochondrial protein basis were decreased in rrd2 callus cultured at 28°C for 3 days (Figure 5, C and D) in two out of three cultures, although the difference was not significant when all three results were included.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: At 22°C, no significant difference in cyt c levels was observed between rrd2 and wild type.
source: At 22°C, however, no significant difference was observed between rrd2 and the wild type.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text referring to the immunoblot analysis.

claim: The difference in cyt c levels between rrd2 and wild type was more pronounced after longer periods of culture at 28°C.
source: Furthermore, we found that the difference in cyt c levels was more pronounced after longer periods of culture at 28°C (Figure 5, E and F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: In rrd2, cyt c maturation activity was affected to a greater extent at higher temperatures in callus.
source: These results indicate that, in rrd2, cyt c maturation activity was affected to a greater extent at higher temperatures, at least in callus, which possesses root-tissue-like properties, possibly explaining the temperature-dependent nature of its phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cyt c quantification data.

claim: In both rrd2 and rid4, the production of certain components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain is hampered by defective mRNA editing.
source: The data reported above demonstrated that, in both rrd2 and rid4, the production of certain components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain is hampered by defective mRNA editing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the editing and protein complex analysis data.

claim: The induction of LRs from wild-type explants in the presence of rotenone, antimycin A, or oligomycin led to LR fasciation.
source: In fact, the induction of LRs from wild-type explants in the presence of rotenone (complex I inhibitor), antimycin A (complex III inhibitor), or oligomycin (complex V inhibitor) led to LR fasciation, providing evidence that electron transport chain defects are the cause of the TDF LR phenotype (Figure 6, A–D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Electron transport chain defects are the cause of the TDF LR phenotype.
source: In fact, the induction of LRs from wild-type explants in the presence of rotenone (complex I inhibitor), antimycin A (complex III inhibitor), or oligomycin (complex V inhibitor) led to LR fasciation, providing evidence that electron transport chain defects are the cause of the TDF LR phenotype (Figure 6, A–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the respiratory inhibitor experiments.

claim: The effect of antimycin A on LR fasciation was stronger at higher temperatures.
source: In addition, we found that the effect of antimycin A was stronger at higher temperatures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The respiratory uncoupler CCCP did not increase LR width.
source: We found that the respiratory uncoupler carbonylcyanide m-chlorophenyl-hydrazone (CCCP) did not increase LR width (Figure 6E), although LR growth inhibition was observed in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: LR growth inhibition was observed with CCCP treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that the respiratory uncoupler carbonylcyanide m-chlorophenyl-hydrazone (CCCP) did not increase LR width (Figure 6E), although LR growth inhibition was observed in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The ROS inducer paraquat triggered a significant fasciation of LRs.
source: whereas the ROS inducer paraquat (PQ) triggered a significant fasciation of LRs (Figure 6, G and H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6G and 6H.

claim: The application of the ROS scavenger ascorbate resulted in a reversal of the LR broadening induced by PQ treatment.
source: Furthermore, the application of the ROS scavenger ascorbate resulted in a reversal of the LR broadening induced by PQ treatment (Figure 6, G and H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6G and 6H.

claim: Ascorbate reversed the LR broadening in the rid4-2 mutant.
source: The same effect was observed against the rid4-2 mutation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text referring to the ascorbate treatment experiment.

claim: The increase in the levels of ROS, but not the decrease in the levels of ATP, acts downstream of defective mitochondrial respiration to promote extra cell division during LR development in the TDF mutants.
source: These data suggest that the increase in the levels of ROS, but not the decrease in the levels of ATP, acts downstream of defective mitochondrial respiration to promote extra cell division during LR development in the TDF mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CCCP, paraquat, and ascorbate experiments.

claim: Local gradient formation of auxin is important for LR initiation and the subsequent organization of the LR primordium.
source: Local gradient formation of auxin is important for LR initiation and the subsequent organization of the LR primordium (Benková et al., 2003; Geldner et al., 2004; Lavenus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Chemical inhibition of auxin polar transport by NPA gave rise to broadened LR primordia reminiscent of fasciated LRs of the TDF mutants.
source: In addition, chemical inhibition of auxin polar transport by naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) gave rise to broadened LR primordia reminiscent of fasciated LRs of the TDF mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Local auxin gradient formation plays a role in restricting proliferative capacity during LR formation.
source: These data indicate a role for local auxin gradient formation in restricting proliferative capacity during LR formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NPA treatment results.

claim: The expression pattern of DR5::GUS at early stages of LR induction did not reveal differences between the control and PQ-treated root segments.
source: The examination of the expression pattern of the auxin-responsive β-glucuronidase marker DR5::GUS (Benková et al., 2003; De Smet et al., 2010; Geldner et al., 2004) at early stages of LR induction, however, did not reveal differences between the control and PQ-treated root segments, whereas treatment with NPA resulted in enhanced expression along the entire root segment (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: ROS-induced LR fasciation is not caused by an impairment in auxin gradient formation.
source: This result indicates that ROS-induced LR fasciation is not caused by an impairment in auxin gradient formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DR5::GUS expression analysis.

claim: Fasciation of LRs in TDF mutants is caused by the excess number of basal cells, which can be detected as early as stage II of LR development.
source: By measuring the cell number and primordium width, we found that fasciation of LRs is caused by the excess number of basal cells, which can be detected as early as stage II of LR development (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The first 48 hr following LR induction are critical for LR fasciation in the TDF mutants.
source: The data are in agreement with the previous result of the temperature-shift experiment, which demonstrated that the first 48 hr following LR induction are critical for LR fasciation in the TDF mutants (Otsuka and Sugiyama, 2012)
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: Stage II to early stage III primordia are formed within 48 hours after LR induction.
source: as stage II to early stage III primordia are formed within this time frame (Figure 2D; Ohtani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of primordium development and cited literature.

claim: Fasciated LR primordia in TDF mutants exhibit specific enlargement of inner root tissues marked by SHR expression.
source: The previous characterization of the TDF mutants also showed that fasciated LR primordia exhibit specific enlargement of inner root tissues marked by the expression of SHORT ROOT (SHR), while the number of cell layers outside the SHR-expressing layer is normal (Otsuka and Sugiyama, 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: The area of SHR expression is first established during stage II, where it is confined to the inner layer of the two-cell layered primordium.
source: A recent study revealed that the area of SHR expression is first established during stage II, where it is confined to the inner layer of the two-cell layered primordium (Goh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: In subsequent stages, SHR is expressed in cell files derived from the inner layer, which develop into the stele of the LR.
source: In subsequent stages, SHR is expressed in cell files derived from the inner layer, which develop into the stele of the LR (Goh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Differentiation into two cell layers at stage II occurs normally in the TDF mutants.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that differentiation into two cell layers at stage II occurs normally in the TDF mutants, and that the increase in the number of cells observed at stage II consequently leads to the expansion of the area of SHR expression in the inner cell layer during LR fasciation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SHR expression pattern and cell number data.

claim: The increase in the number of cells observed at stage II leads to the expansion of the area of SHR expression in the inner cell layer during LR fasciation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that differentiation into two cell layers at stage II occurs normally in the TDF mutants, and that the increase in the number of cells observed at stage II consequently leads to the expansion of the area of SHR expression in the inner cell layer during LR fasciation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SHR expression pattern and cell number data.

claim: In plant mitochondria, immature 3´ extremities of mRNA, together with irregular RNAs, are polyadenylated before they are degraded by mitochondrial polynucleotide phosphorylase (mtPNPase).
source: In plant mitochondria, immature 3´ extremities of mRNA, together with irregular RNAs, such as 3´ misprocessed mRNAs, rRNA maturation by-products, and cryptic transcripts, are known to be polyadenylated before they are degraded by mitochondrial polynucleotide phosphorylase (mtPNPase) (Holec et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Down-regulation of mtPNPase in Arabidopsis results in the accumulation of long preprocessed mRNAs and irregular RNAs, the majority of which are polyadenylated.
source: In fact, down-regulation of mtPNPase in Arabidopsis results in the accumulation of long preprocessed mRNAs, as well as irregular RNAs, the majority of which are polyadenylated (Holec et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: In rrd1, unusually long preprocessed mRNAs do not seem to accumulate.
source: In rrd1, unusually long preprocessed mRNAs do not seem to accumulate, as the size of RACE-PAT assay products (Figure 3D) corresponded to that of previously reported mature transcript 3´ ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RACE-PAT assay results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Total mitochondrial mRNA levels were unelevated in rrd1.
source: Total mitochondrial mRNA levels were unelevated in rrd1 (Figure 3B), suggesting that RRD1 is not involved in controlling mRNA abundance by promoting their degradation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RRD1 is not involved in controlling mRNA abundance by promoting their degradation.
source: Total mitochondrial mRNA levels were unelevated in rrd1 (Figure 3B), suggesting that RRD1 is not involved in controlling mRNA abundance by promoting their degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the total mRNA level data.

claim: RRD1 plays a distinct role from mtPNPase and seems to be specifically involved in 3´ processing of near-matured mRNA.
source: Based on these considerations, we concluded that RRD1 plays a distinct role from mtPNPase and seems to be specifically involved in 3´ processing of near-matured mRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison with mtPNPase function.

claim: RRD1 requires additional factors for its participation in poly(A) tail removal.
source: The absence of three out of the four catalytic amino acids (DEDD) that are essential for ribonuclease activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Reverdatto et al., 2004), together with the apparent lack of deadenylase activity of the recombinant RRD1 protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, D and E), indicated that RRD1 requires additional factors for its participation in poly(A) tail removal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of catalytic residues and deadenylase activity.

claim: The exact impact of the altered poly(A) status of mRNAs in mitochondria on electron transport in rrd1 remains unclear.
source: However, the exact impact of the altered poly(A) status of mRNAs in mitochondria on electron transport in rrd1 remains unclear.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty.

claim: No significant difference in respiratory chain composition has been detected in rrd1 to date.
source: Unlike the AtPARN/AHG2 loss-of-function mutant ahg2, which shows a reduction in complex III levels (Hirayama et al., 2013), no significant difference in respiratory chain composition has been detected in rrd1 to date (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: More than 50 out of approximately 200 PLS-class PPR proteins in Arabidopsis have been identified as C-to-U editing factors of mitochondria or plastid RNA.
source: A predominant role for PLS-class PPR proteins in RNA editing has been demonstrated with more than 50 out of a total of approximately 200 of these proteins in Arabidopsis having been identified as C-to-U editing factors of mitochondria or plastid RNA (Kobayashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: ccb2 and ccb3 encode a multisubunit ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein involved in the maturation of mono hemic c-type cytochromes.
source: Both ccb2 (also known as ccb206, ccmB, ABCI2, and AtMg00110) and ccb3 (also known as ccb256, ccmC, ABCI3, and AtMg00900) encode a multisubunit ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein, which are involved in the maturation of mono hemic c-type cytochromes, the soluble cyt c, and the membrane-bound cyt c1 of complex III (Giegé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: ccb3-575C was previously reported as a target of RRD2/CWM2.
source: Of the two editing sites, ccb3-575C was previously reported as a target of RRD2/CWM2 (Hu et al., 2016), whereas ccb2-71C is a newly discovered target.
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature.

claim: ccb2-71C is a newly discovered target of RRD2/CWM2.
source: Of the two editing sites, ccb3-575C was previously reported as a target of RRD2/CWM2 (Hu et al., 2016), whereas ccb2-71C is a newly discovered target.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: A decrease in the level of cyt c was detected in rrd2, which is consistent with that reported previously for cwm2.
source: A decrease in the level of cyt c was detected in rrd2, which is consistent with that reported previously for cwm2 (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and compared with previous literature.

claim: RRD2/CWM2 plays a role in cyt c maturation via the RNA editing of cyt c biogenesis factors.
source: The data demonstrated the role of RRD2/CWM2 in cyt c maturation via the RNA editing of cyt c biogenesis factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the editing and cyt c level data.

claim: atp4 encodes the peripheral stalk protein (subunit b) of the mitochondrial ATP synthase complex (complex V).
source: atp4 (also known as orf25, AtMg00640) encodes the peripheral stalk protein (subunit b) of the mitochondrial ATP synthase complex (complex V) (Heazlewood et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: rpl5, rps3, and rps4 encode mitochondrial ribosome proteins.
source: rpl5, rps3, and rps4 encode mitochondrial ribosome proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The formation of complex V could be disrupted by defective RNA editing at a single site of a subunit gene.
source: This is similar to the organelle transcript processing 87 (otp87) mutant of Arabidopsis, in which editing of atp1-1178C is deficient (Takenaka et al., 2019). These data showed that the formation of complex V could be disrupted by defective RNA editing at a single site of a subunit gene.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rid4 data and comparison with the otp87 mutant.

claim: C-to-U editing of the rps4 transcript at rps4-377 affects mitochondrial ribosome assembly in the grs1 mutant.
source: Considering that the C-to-U editing of the rps4 transcript at a different site (rps4-377) has been shown to affect mitochondrial ribosome assembly in the growing slowly 1 (grs1) mutant (Takenaka et al., 2019), it is possible that the rid4 mutation also has an impact on the mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature and used for speculation.

claim: It is possible that the rid4 mutation has an impact on the mitochondrial ribosome.
source: Considering that the C-to-U editing of the rps4 transcript at a different site (rps4-377) has been shown to affect mitochondrial ribosome assembly in the growing slowly 1 (grs1) mutant (Takenaka et al., 2019), it is possible that the rid4 mutation also has an impact on the mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence: This is speculation based on the editing defects in ribosomal protein genes.

claim: The PPR code enables the matching of PPR proteins to their candidate editing targets, and vice versa.
source: By mapping these residues of previously reported RNA-editing PPR proteins to their binding sites, which are located 5' upstream of the editing sites, the so-called 'PPR code' has been elucidated, thus enabling the matching of PPR proteins to their candidate editing targets, and vice versa (Kobayashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: According to the PPR code prediction, RID4 was highly ranked as a potential binding protein of atp4-395C, rpl5-58C, and rps4-332C.
source: According to the recently refined PPR code prediction (Kobayashi et al., 2019), RID4 was highly ranked as a potential binding protein of atp4-395C (18th, p=4.35 × 10–2), rpl5-58C (5th, p=3.04 × 10–2) and rps4-332C (2nd, p=4.06 × 10–3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on computational prediction.

claim: atp4-395C, rpl5-58C, and rps4-332C were among the predicted editing sites of RID4.
source: Conversely, these sites were among the predicted editing sites of RID4 (p<0.05) (Kobayashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on computational prediction.

claim: The newly identified RRD2 binding site (ccb2-71C) ranked very low in the PPR code prediction.
source: With regard to RRD2, however, the newly identified binding site (ccb2-71C) ranked very low, despite the incorporation of RRD2/CWM2 binding to ccb3-575C as learning data for the PPR code prediction (Kobayashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on computational prediction.

claim: The discrepancy in PPR code prediction for RRD2 may be related to the unusual arrangement of PPR motifs in RRD2.
source: This discrepancy may be related to the unusual arrangement of PPR motifs in RRD2, in which repeats of SS motifs are prevalent, in contrast to canonical PLS-class PPRs, which follow the (P1-L1-S1)n-P2-L2-S2 pattern, such as RID4 (Figure 2A; Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural features of RRD2.

claim: The rrd1 mutation causes a truncation of the C-terminal domain of the RRD1 protein.
source: The rrd1 mutation causes a truncation of the C-terminal domain of the RRD1 protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In rrd1, RRD1 is partially functional at least at the permissive temperature, and its activity is more severely affected at the non-permissive temperature.
source: This finding, together with the enhancement of poly(A)+ mitochondrial mRNA accumulation at elevated temperatures (Figure 3D), implies that, in rrd1, RRD1 is partially functional at least at the permissive temperature, and that its activity is more severely affected at the non-permissive temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the mutation and the temperature-dependent accumulation of poly(A)+ mRNA.

claim: The rrd2 and rid4-1 mutations likely result in the total loss of their functions.
source: In contrast, the rrd2 and rid4-1 mutations introduce a stop codon close to the N-terminus of RRD2 and RID4, respectively, likely resulting in the total loss of their functions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the position of the mutations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The complete abolishment of RNA editing of the RRD2 and RID4 target sites in the rrd2 and rid4-1 mutants, regardless of temperature, supports the idea that these mutations result in total loss of function.
source: The complete abolishment of RNA editing of the RRD2 and RID4 target sites in the rrd2 and rid4-1 mutants, regardless of temperature (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), further supported this idea.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In rrd2, deficient cyt c biogenesis was observed only at high temperature.
source: However, in rrd2, deficient cyt c biogenesis was observed only at high temperature (Figure 5, C and D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The temperature sensitivity of cyt c biogenesis in rrd2 might be accounted for by the temperature sensitivity of the function of either ccb2 or ccb3.
source: This might be accounted for by the temperature sensitivity of the function of either ccb2 or ccb3, which exhibit alteration of the amino acid sequence in rrd2, because of impaired RNA editing (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is speculation based on the editing defects and their consequences.

claim: In rid4-1, a huge reduction in complex V biosynthesis was observed both at permissive and non-permissive temperatures.
source: In rid4-1, a huge reduction in complex V biosynthesis was observed both at permissive and non-permissive temperatures (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Unlike rrd1 and rrd2, rid4-1 is constitutively impaired in mitochondrial function.
source: Thus, unlike rrd1 and rrd2, rid4-1 is constitutively impaired in mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complex V data.

claim: Fasciation of LRs observed in the wild type treated with antimycin A was more pronounced at higher temperatures.
source: Our study also found that fasciation of LRs observed in the wild type treated with the respiratory inhibitor antimycin A was more pronounced at higher temperatures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondrial impairment and elevated temperature both contribute to LR fasciation in the TDF mutants.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that mitochondrial impairment and elevated temperature both contribute to LR fasciation in the TDF mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temperature-dependent effects of antimycin A and the constitutive mitochondrial defects in rid4-1.

claim: Reduced ATP production seems unlikely to be the cause of LR fasciation.
source: Given the lack of LR fasciation after treatment with the mitochondrial uncoupler CCCP (Figure 6, E and F), reduced ATP production seems unlikely to be the cause of LR fasciation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CCCP treatment results.

claim: The huge reduction in complex V levels observed in rid4 does not lead to LR fasciation at the permissive temperature.
source: The fact that the huge reduction in complex V levels observed in rid4 (Figure 5B) does not lead to LR fasciation at the permissive temperature (Otsuka and Sugiyama, 2012) is also supportive of this idea.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complex V data and the phenotype at permissive temperature.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS generation is the potential trigger of LR fasciation.
source: Experiments using the ROS inducer PQ and the antioxidant ascorbate (Figure 6, G and H) pointed to mitochondrial ROS generation as the potential trigger of LR fasciation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PQ and ascorbate experiments.

claim: Enhanced cell division was observed after the application of the ROS inducer alloxan during auxin-induced LR formation.
source: A previous study also observed enhanced cell division after the application of another ROS inducer, alloxan, during auxin-induced LR formation (Pasternak et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature.

claim: All three respiratory inhibitors used in the study (rotenone, antimycin A, and oligomycin) are potent inducers of oxidative stress.
source: In agreement with this 'ROS hypothesis', all three respiratory inhibitors used in our study (rotenone, antimycin A, and oligomycin) are potent inducers of oxidative stress (Willems et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: ROS have been implicated in stress-induced morphogenic responses (SIMR).
source: ROS have been implicated in stress-induced morphogenic responses (SIMR) (Potters et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Altered auxin levels and/or distribution have been proposed as potential mediators in the modulation of cell proliferation in response to oxidative stress.
source: Several studies have shown the involvement of phytohormonal regulation in ROS-triggered SIMR. Altered auxin levels and/or distribution have been proposed as potential mediators in the modulation of cell proliferation in response to oxidative stress (Pasternak et al., 2005; Potters et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Several recent studies have found antagonistic interactions between auxin signaling and mitochondrial ROS.
source: Several recent studies have found antagonistic interactions between auxin signaling and mitochondrial ROS (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The centripetal auxin-gradient formation in early-stage LR primordia is thought to contribute to the organization of the LR primordium.
source: Auxin is a critical factor in LR development, and the centripetal auxin-gradient formation in early-stage LR primordia is thought to contribute to the organization of the LR primordium (Benková et al., 2003; Geldner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Further studies of LR fasciation caused by oxidative stress will elucidate novel aspects of the control of cell proliferation during plant organogenesis.
source: Further studies of LR fasciation caused by oxidative stress will elucidate novel aspects of the control of cell proliferation during plant organogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: ROS has recently emerged as a potential signal required for plant physiology and development under normal conditions.
source: Apart from its role in stress response, ROS has recently emerged as a potential signal in and of itself that is required for plant physiology and development under normal conditions (Mittler, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: In the primary root, a regulatory mechanism of meristem size involving spatial zoning of different types of apoplastic ROS has been proposed.
source: In the primary root, a regulatory mechanism of meristem size involving spatial zoning of different types of apoplastic ROS has been proposed, whereby O2•- promotes cell proliferation in the meristematic zone, while H2O2 induces cell differentiation in the elongation zone (Tsukagoshi et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: UPBEAT1 (UPB1) is suggested to regulate the transition between the meristematic zone and elongation zone via the suppression of extracellular peroxidase activity.
source: The transcription factor UPBEAT1 (UPB1) is suggested to regulate the transition between the two zones, via the suppression of extracellular peroxidase activity in the elongation zone (Tsukagoshi et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: During LR formation, factors involved in apoplastic ROS regulation, UPB1 and MYB36, as well as some members of the RBOH family, are expressed in the periphery of the LR primordium.
source: Interestingly, during LR formation, factors involved in apoplastic ROS regulation, UPB1 and another transcription factor MYB36, as well as some members of the RESPIRATORY BURST OXIDASE HOMOLOG (RBOH) family, are expressed in the periphery of the LR primordium (Fernández-Marcos et al., 2017; Manzano et al., 2014; Orman-Ligeza et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The role of apoplastic ROS in controlling the proliferation-to-differentiation transition in the LR boundary remains largely speculative.
source: however, the role of apoplastic ROS in controlling the proliferation-to-differentiation transition in the LR boundary remains largely speculative.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty.

claim: Whether mitochondrial disorders caused by the TDF mutations have an impact on apoplastic ROS remains to be investigated.
source: Whether mitochondrial disorders caused by the TDF mutations have an impact on apoplastic ROS also remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty.

claim: Reactive carbonyl species (RCS) were found to mediate auxin signaling in a feed-forward manner during LR formation.
source: In addition, reactive carbonyl species (RCS), which are lipid peroxidation products generated by ROS, were found to mediate auxin signaling in a feed-forward manner during LR formation (Biswas et al., 2019; Mano et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: No apparent morphological LR phenotype has been observed in RCS-treated plants.
source: however, no apparent morphological LR phenotype has been observed in RCS-treated plants.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: The possible involvement of RCS in the TDF LR phenotype awaits further testing.
source: The possible involvement of RCS in the TDF LR phenotype awaits further testing.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty.

claim: Studies of C-to-U editing PPR protein genes have led to a collection of about 100 mutants.
source: In particular, studies of C-to-U editing PPR protein genes have led to a collection of about 100 mutants, among which RNA-editing mutants are available for most mitochondrial genes (Takenaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The majority of mutations in mitochondrial RNA processing factors confer visible phenotypes, such as growth retardation, impaired embryo development, late flowering, or reduced pollen sterility.
source: The majority of the mutations confer visible phenotypes, such as growth retardation, impaired embryo development, late flowering, or reduced pollen sterility (Takenaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Similar developmental defects are observed in mutants of genes encoding other mitochondrial proteins, including ndufs4, rpoTmp, and atphb3.
source: Similar developmental defects are also observed in mutants of genes encoding other mitochondrial proteins, including ndufs4 (complex I mutant), rpoTmp (RNA polymerase mutant), and atphb3 (prohibitin mutant) (Van Aken et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Mitochondria play a supportive role in plant growth, presumably by supplying energy through oxidative phosphorylation.
source: These results suggest that mitochondria play a supportive role in plant growth, presumably by supplying energy through oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of mitochondrial mutants.

claim: Mitochondrial RNA processing is required for preventing extra cell division during LR primordium formation.
source: In this study, however, we found that mitochondrial RNA processing is required for preventing extra cell division during LR primordium formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Mitochondrial gene expression not only supports active cell proliferation for growth and development but also participates in the local fine-tuning of organ morphogenesis by restricting cell proliferation.
source: This suggests that mitochondrial gene expression not only supports active cell proliferation for growth and development but also participates in the local fine-tuning of organ morphogenesis by restricting cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The study identified an unexpected link between mitochondrial RNA processing and the primordial size control at the early stage of LR development, probably mediated by changes in the level of mitochondrial ROS.
source: In summary, our study identified an unexpected link between mitochondrial RNA processing and the primordial size control at the early stage of LR development, probably mediated by changes in the level of mitochondrial ROS.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The discovery provides a novel clue for the physiological significance of mitochondrial activities in the restrictive regulation of cell division required for the proper morphogenesis of plant organs.
source: This finding provides a novel clue for the physiological significance of mitochondrial activities in the restrictive regulation of cell division required for the proper morphogenesis of plant organs.
evidence: This is a statement of the broader significance of the findings.
